These actions express not merely the simple desire of these  students to use public lunch counters, but are more fundamentally, an  understandable protest by citizens of South Carolina against continued  unequal treatment in the use of public facilities and services. All  South Carolinians should understand that no group of citizens will  permanently accept less than the full rights and courtesies enjoyed by  other citizens.    2. These pretests for the most part have been orderly and peaceful  demonstrations.    3┬╗ Repression of such peaceful demonstrations by force or by new  legislation would only compound our present difficulties.    U. The board commends both the city police and the officials wherever  they have handled these demonstrations in an impartial professional  manner.    5. Dear Mr. President:    December 11, 1961    Having exhausted all other likely approaches,  I am appealing for any assistance you may be able  to give as tituler head of our Party in disposing  of the matter explained in the attached statement.    The predicament was well known to the following  persons before the i960 General Election, each of  whom was given a detailed statement of the operations:    The Honorables William L. Dawson, Frank Reeves,  Louis E. Martin ┬ºnd Oliver W, Hill.    Additional detailed statements and letters were  later filed with the Honorables Robert Shriver, Steve  Smith, and John M. Bailey. None of these has replied,  however.    The matter, recently, was called to the attention  of Senator Olin D. Johnston, our senior Senator, and  I understand that his office will try to have it looked  into, but with a reluctance to do so because it is a  matter of the National Democratic Committee. A spokesman  for his office advises that Senator Johnston thinks the  matter should be settled forthwith. Congressman Dawson  has expressed the same opinion to me personally.    It is now a desperate situation for me personally.  I would be most grateful for whatever assistance you  will be kind enough to give. Another taxi driver came up  and said go back to the Pan Am desk and let them straighten you out. This they did.    In Lisbon there was some big gathering going on and almost all of the hotels  were full. The man at the desk apologized for having to send me so far and to a  obscure hotel. Having met the ugly practice of discrimination all of ny life in one  way or another, I was quite suspicious especiall with the long drive and the dark  front of the hotel when we arrived. However, after the long delay in waking the  hotel keeper up we were permitted to come in and there they talked. During the time while we were trying to get straight other passangers from the same  plane came in. Then all the suspicion was cleared from ny mind that I was descriminated  against. It was a case of hotel shortage. I stayed in Hotel Urgeirica.    While writing this report I have received a letter from Pan American World Airways.  It says, "Dear Father DeLaine: It is unfortunate that the schedule Hight 153--could  not be met and I sincerely regrat the inconvenience it caused you. As you know, the  weather prevented us from operating as planned on that occasion. In the interest of  safety, we had no alternative. I hope that we may have the continued pleasure of  serving you and that the next time it will be under more favorable circumstances.    Sincerely,    John T. Shannon, Division Manager.    In Lisbon at the Port of Embarkation the formalities of the Government didnΓÇÖt  seem so boring but when we reached Madrid, Spain, the Red Tape and formalitied felt  like it was to the extreme. Then what made it worse were the followingj 1. I was  anxious to get to the desk to have ny ticket confirmed before the plane left for  Basalonia, Spain. 2. There was a suspicious man among the passangers and a loud  mouth woman. Both of them were confusing to both the passangers and the officers.  The man inpressed me that he was running away from some crime and he was almost  vicious. The Stewaress tried to take him to another place for something and he  shouted at her like she had committed some crime. I have often been disgusted and  ahamed of the stupid ignorance of some of our people but this was a clear cut example  that stupidity or uncouthness is not limited to race or color. Finally this man was  lost in the rush. The woman was not his wife as first we believed. She travelled on  with us. Ify flight was confirmed on the Iberiane Line and when we reached Basalonia  Spain then we had another nauseating embarkation formalities to go through.    We were guided in the lounge where we could rest and buy souviners and drinks.  I decided to get ma a soda. The man gave ma a sale ticket with lip on it. I gave  him 150 but he was not satisfied and wanted more. I wanted ny change, rather than  have ary confusion I opened rry hand and he took 200 and gave me back 10. Therefore,  I concluded that 190 is 110 in Spanish money.    Our stay at Rome was brief. Only about three hours was the schedule but we had  to remain there about six hours. The EL AL, The Israel plane was late but finally  it came. The embarkation system for transit passangers seems to be the best in Rome  of ary of the places I had formally stopped in. We did not have to go through all  of that formality to change planes.    Israel being a young nation and I was not so famelia with the EL AL Israel Line  I was fearful that it would be a little unkept plane. But when we boarded it ny mind  changed. Iw Mas one of the Big Boren Jet Planes. Over the loud speaker the it was  announced that we are going to fly at an altitude of 32 to 33 thousand feet in the  air at a speed of 600 miles per hour. MENACHEMΓÇÖS ROOM    The night man took me up to a room and before entering it he took pride in  pointing at the sign on the door. It was written in more than one languages. I could  read the Bnglish, It said, "Menachem Begin, Commander of the Irgun Zewaileumi lived  in this room in the period of the Jewish Resistance Movement". I was quite happy with  my room on the back with ny single bed. All night long I could hear the lashing of  the waves against the shore of the Mediterrenian Sea. Whenever I desired I could sit  and look over the sea night or day.    At breakfast I was somewhat lost. I sat and waited on some one to come and take  ny order but no one came. Finally I asked one for breakfast and he pointed to the  cold food and said it is self service. I finally asked for coffee and egg and got it.  At lunch I cal 1 ed for some meat and when he served it he told me he would have  to serve it on another table. A flag looking like the United States Flag was at ny table  but I did not know what was the significence of it. Finally he place the U.S. Flag at a  table opposite me. Then I got up and brough a U.S.Flag and placed it on ny table.  The man came to me and said, "This is the Liberian Flag". I s id yes I know it but  I am An American. By coming directly from Liberia they had me signed up as a Liberian.  The Flag is like the U.S. Flag but only one star is in the corner of it.    I went to the Liberian Embassy. There I found Honerable Mr. Earnest Yancy packing  up getting ready to come to New York and for a while Join the Liberian team at the  U.N. He was leaving the AmbassadorΓÇÖs business in the hand of the Charge M D'AFFAIRS,  Mr. James Stevens. They extended me such a warm welcome. Original Transcript: IMPROVED STRUCTUREΓÇöRecent exterior improvements to Emanuel African Methodist  Episcopal church are illustrated in this recent photograph.    <$>     Charleston Negro  Believed About h    (EditorΓÇÖs note: The accompanying article was prepared by the  Rev. Dr. Frank R. Veal, pastor  of. Emanuel church, for The  News and Courier.)    By DR. FRANK R. VEAL    Emanuel African Methodist  Episcopal church, at 108-114 Calhoun street, has occupied this site  for more than 100 years. Prior to  use of the present site the congregation was located in the neighborhood of Hanover and Amherst  streets.    Emanuel church is believed to  be about 160 years old. In its lifetime it has had three different  names: the African church, the  Bethel circuit and Emanuel African Methodist Episcopal church.    Birth of Emanuel was paralleled  by birth of similar religious and  social organizations in Boston and  Philadelphia. Those in Philadelphia  and Boston were called the Free    Congregation  0 Years Old    African society and the one in  Charleston was called the African  church. Difference in these early  movements lies in the fact that  only free negroes, though there  were many slaves in Philadelphia  and Boston, were taken into the  societies in those cities.    In Charleston, both slaves and  free negroes were permitted to  join. Both groups were stimulated  by two common causes, but a third  cause gave impetus to the Charleston group. The third cause revolved  around the dead.    Methodists began to gain ground  in South Carolina with the close of  the Revolutionary war. The  Methodist class system made it  easy for the slaves to gather after  working hours and the system  fitted well into the small quarters  of free negroes. Those slaves who  had confessed religion were given  special privileges when members  of their Methodist faith were dead.  They were permitted to attend  ΓÇ£wakesΓÇ¥ and funerals.    Therefore, whether they had  religion or not, any number of  slaves joined the chrch so that  these advantages might be used.  As early as 1787, there were more  than 6,000 negroes professing the  Methodist faith in Charleston. It    was about this time that about 3,-  800 free and slave negroes set up  their own church and called it the  African church.    It is not safe to say that these  negroes felt themselves separate  from the Mother Church at first.  They never did set up a new doctrine. The only thing they did that  was new was the founding of a  new cemetery and a new location  for the congregation to meet.    The first congregation of the  African church and the cemetery  were located somewhere in the  neighborhood of Hanover and Amherst streets.    One may wonder where the negroes in that day obtained money  to purchase land and lumber to  build a church and a cemetery.  But it must be remembered that  Charleston gave great opportunity  to free negroes during slavery. For  example, in 1840, one negro paid  taxes on property worth about  $648,000. There were many negro  slaveholders holding up to 200  slaves in the Charleston area.    Yet, we must remember that  many of the negroes participating  in the church movement had other  motives than religion. The influence of Haiti and other Latin  American insurrections had much  effect upon the North Amerian  negro and we can see much of this  in the early life of Emanuel church.    The founders of Emanuel were  both local preachers and laymen.  The name of one of the noted  founders is part of American history. The insurrectionist leader,  Denmark Vesey, was one of the  founders of Emanuel church.    Another great character was a  local preacher by the name of  Morris Brown, who later became a  bishop in the African Methodist  Episcopal church.    Vesey was a very religious person. He obtained his freedom with  money he had won in a lottery. He  was later a leader among the laymen in the beginning of the church.  He was very active from 1790 up  to his conviction as leader of the    slave insurrection of 1822.    In 1816, the Free African Society  of the North became the African  Methodist Episcopal church. The  African Church of Charleston  joihed this new organization in  1818 and the general conference of  1820 named the Charleston congregation the Bethel circuit. This  name was retained until 1865.    The first great setback to  Emanuel church came soon after  she had joined the A. M. E. church.  Vesey became involved in a plot  which was proved beyond a doubt  to be designed to lead to insurrection to free all the slaves in    Charleston. When the city of    Charleston became convinced that  Vesey had used the church to cover  up his movements, the church *  was ordered to close.    The church would have fared ;  better had it obeyed the order,  but the membership did not believe <  Vesey and some others were guil- *  ty. In 1822, Vesey attempted his  insurrection and the church was \\\\  burned down. After the tension had j  subsided, the church was rebuilt  and remained open until 1834, when .  the states throughout the South *  ordered all negro churches closed. (    This new law was due to a plot  similar to that of VeseyΓÇÖs and was \\\\  led by a negro in Virginia named  Nat Turner. The congregation of  Emanuel went underground. Some  members went into the Presbyterian church and remained there  until 1865.    Some time between 1834 and 1865  the members of the Bethel circuit  bought the present site of Emanuel. This property was purchased  because that side of Calhoun 3  street was territory set aside for .  free negroes. . j    Teaching of negroes and religious services at that time were  carried on in secret. Many times  they were exposed and many free  negroes were shipped from the  state. Among this group probably  was the most outstanding negro  educator in American history,  Daniel Payne. This condition existed until 1865.    In April, 1865. at the close of the  War Between the States, many  negro preachers were sent to the  South to help the ex-slaves adjust  themselves to ethics, morals and  responsibilities of their new state  in American life.    The Rev. Richard Cain was sent  to Charleston. He reopened the  Bethel Circuit and named it  Emanuel. Emanuel grew rapidly  under Cain and became the mother church of this section, sending  missionaries throughout the South.    New lots were bought adjoining  the old lot. A new church was built  and completed in 1872. This structure remained until the earthquake  of 1886.    The present structure was built  during the pastorate of the late Γûá  Rev. Dr. L. R. Nichols, whose son  is now a bishop in the A. M. E.  church. The present restoration  was completed this year during 1  the pastorate of the Rev. Dr.  Frank R. Veal. Cost of redecoration  of the church and purchase of a  parsonage was $47,467.    The congregation has an enrolled  membership of 2.400 persons. It  plans to redecorate the interior of  the church upstairs and downstairs  at a cost of $20,000. The downstairs  will be changed to meet the program of the congregation.    The Charleston chamber of commerce presented the congregation  a certificate for the work done on  the building as an outstanding improvement in Charleston last year. '    Emanuel has a junior church with '  a full-time pastor, the Rev. J. S.  Roper. The junior church holds its  weekly services on Monday due to  lack of space on Sunday. The  church holds two prayer services  each week. It maintains a welfare  board and owns two large ceme-  eries in upper Meeting street.
